questions.question: A client's creatinine rose from 0.7 to 1.1 mg/dL within 48 hours. Which interpretation is best?
choices: This is normal because 1.1 mg/dL is within many laboratory reference ranges
The 0.4 mg/dL increase meets a common AKI recognition threshold and needs evaluation
Only urine output can identify AKI
The client has CKD because the current creatinine is above baseline
questions.explanation: An increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours meets a common AKI criterion. Baseline and time course matter more than whether the current value falls in a broad reference range.

questions.question: A 70-kg hospitalized adult has produced 25 mL of urine each hour for seven hours. What should the RN recognize?
choices: The output is adequate because some urine is present
The client has confirmed permanent kidney failure
The output is below 0.5 mL/kg/hour and warrants prompt AKI assessment
Creatinine must rise before urine output is meaningful
questions.explanation: For 70 kg, 0.5 mL/kg/hour is 35 mL/hour. Sustained output of 25 mL/hour is oliguria; verify measurement and assess perfusion, obstruction, medications, and other causes.

questions.question: A client with AKI has potassium 6.4 mEq/L, new weakness, and ECG changes. Which problem has highest priority?
choices: Potentially life-threatening dysrhythmia from hyperkalemia
Long-term dietary preferences
An isolated need for a routine annual eGFR test
A delayed outpatient nutrition referral
questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia with symptoms and ECG changes can rapidly cause fatal arrhythmia. Assess the client and rhythm, urgently escalate, and implement the prescribed emergency plan.

questions.question: A client with heart failure has oliguria, crackles, increasing oxygen need, and marked edema. What is the safest initial reasoning?
choices: Give a large fluid bolus automatically because all oliguria means dehydration
Assume the low urine output proves a blocked catheter
Assess perfusion and congestion together and escalate before adding fluid
Ignore the urine output because edema is present
questions.explanation: Low effective kidney perfusion may coexist with fluid overload. A reflex fluid bolus could worsen pulmonary edema; the RN assesses both circulation and congestion and follows the individualized plan.

questions.question: A client suddenly stops producing urine after a urinary catheter was repositioned. Which action should the RN take first?
choices: Immediately diagnose intrinsic kidney injury
Check the collection system and catheter for kinks or obstruction while assessing the client
Assume the kidneys have permanently stopped functioning
Document zero output and wait until the next shift
questions.explanation: An abrupt change after catheter manipulation may reflect a measurement or drainage problem. Verify patency and assess the client promptly before attributing the finding to kidney tissue injury.

questions.question: Which finding best supports a diagnosis of CKD rather than one isolated abnormal test?
choices: A single low eGFR during an acute illness
A one-time concentrated urine sample
Persistent kidney-function or damage abnormality for more than three months
One mildly elevated creatinine with no prior data
questions.explanation: CKD requires evidence of kidney abnormality for more than three months. A single result during acute illness may represent AKI or a transient finding and needs contextual follow-up.

questions.question: A client has eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m² but repeatedly elevated urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. What does this mean?
choices: Preserved eGFR rules out kidney damage
Albuminuria may show kidney damage even when eGFR is relatively preserved
Urine albumin has no role in CKD evaluation
Only blood urea nitrogen can identify early CKD
questions.explanation: Kidney damage may be present before substantial eGFR reduction. Persistent albuminuria is a key marker, and CKD classification considers both GFR and albuminuria.

questions.question: Which plan best reduces avoidable harm for a client with AKI?
choices: Review volume status, treat the cause, reconcile medicines and kidney dosing, and trend urine and laboratory results
Give NSAIDs routinely for any pain without checking kidney risk
Stop every chronic kidney-protective drug independently
Use a diuretic solely to make the urine-output number look better
questions.explanation: AKI care depends on cause and volume status while preventing nephrotoxic exposure and drug accumulation. Medication holds or adjustments require individualized orders and monitoring.

questions.question: A client with AKI has pulmonary edema despite medical therapy and worsening acidosis. Which statement is most appropriate?
choices: Kidney replacement therapy is never considered until creatinine reaches one fixed number
Only urine color determines treatment urgency
The clinical complications justify urgent nephrology discussion about kidney replacement therapy
A normal platelet count excludes severe AKI
questions.explanation: Refractory fluid overload or severe acid–base and electrolyte disturbance can require kidney replacement therapy. The decision considers the whole patient rather than a single creatinine cutoff.

questions.question: After treating suspected prerenal AKI, which evaluation is most complete?
choices: Record one higher urine-output hour and declare recovery
Trend urine output, perfusion, breathing, weight, electrolytes, creatinine, and follow-up needs
Stop reviewing medication doses once blood pressure rises
Use a single eGFR during rapidly changing creatinine as an exact measure of recovery
questions.explanation: Recovery assessment requires clinical and laboratory trends, fluid balance, medication safety, and follow-up. One urine-output value or non–steady-state eGFR cannot establish full recovery.
